The Councilor’s gate key suited this; its heavy bit hung downward. The baron balanced the key’s bow on his right forefinger, where it hung loose, each pulse moving it; if not, he subtly turned it. Each turn indicated a letter, from A onward. When the first letter of a word was found, the key swung opposite for the next, spelling words, sentences, answers. It was mere trickery, amusing—the Councilor’s first thought, but he grew engrossed.

“Husband! Husband!” cried Mrs. Councilor. “The Westgate closes at twelve! We’ve only a quarter-hour to hurry.” They hastened, but others outpaced them. They neared the guardhouse as the clock struck twelve and gates slammed, locking many out, including the Councilor, his wife, maid, tea service, and empty basket. Some stood frightened, others vexed. What to do? Luckily, a recent ordinance left the Northgate unlocked at night, allowing pedestrians through. The road there was long, but the weather was fine, starlight and shooting stars bright, frogs croaking in ditches. The group sang song after song, but the Councilor sang not, nor looked at stars or his feet. He fell full-length by a ditch. One might think him drunk, but it was the key, not punch, that dizzyed him, turning in his mind. They reached the Northgate, slipped across the bridge into the city. “Now I’m relieved,” said Mrs. Councilor. “Here’s our gate.” “But where’s the key?” said the Councilor. Not in back or side pocket. “Good gracious!” cried his wife. “Haven’t you it? You lost it after the Baron’s trick! How will we enter? The bell cord broke today, and the watchman hasn’t our key. We’re hopeless!” The maid wept. Only the Councilor kept calm. “We must break the grocer’s windowpane downstairs,” he said, “rouse him, and get in.” He broke one pane, then two. “Petersen!” he shouted, poking his umbrella handle through. The grocer’s daughter screamed. The grocer flung open his shop door, crying, “Watchman!” Before recognizing the Councilor’s family, the watchman whistled, another answered, people appeared at windows. “Where’s the fire? What’s the excitement?” they asked, even after the Councilor was inside. There he removed his overcoat—and in the lining lay the gate key, not in the pocket but through a hole that shouldn’t have been there.

From that night, the gate key gained unique importance, whether taken out or kept home, for the Councilor would show his cleverness by making it answer questions. He’d think of likely answers and let the key seem to give them. At last, he believed in its power. Not so the Pharmacist, a young relative of Mrs. Councilor. He had a critical mind; as a schoolboy, he’d submitted unsigned critiques of books and theater. A bel esprit, he believed not in spirits, least of all key spirits. “Yes, I believe,” he said, “blessed Mr. Councilor, in gate keys and all key spirits as firmly as in that new science of table-turning and spirits in furniture. Have you heard? I doubted—I’m a skeptic—but a reliable foreign paper converted me with a dreadful tale. Councilor, imagine! Two clever children saw their parents raise spirits in a dining table. Alone, they tried rubbing life into an old chest. Life came; a spirit awoke but tolerated not children’s commands; it arose, the chest creaked, shot out drawers, and with wooden legs put each child in a drawer. It ran out the door, down stairs, into the street, to the canal, jumped in, and drowned both. The little bodies were buried; the chest was tried for murder and burned in the market! I read this in a foreign paper; I invented it not. It’s truth, and may the key take me if it lies! I swear on my oath!”

The Councilor found this too coarse a jest. They never agreed on the key. The Pharmacist was key-ignorant. The Councilor advanced in key knowledge; the key was his diversion and wisdom channel. One evening, as he undressed for bed, a knock came: the downstairs shopkeeper, also half-dressed, calling late. He’d had a thought he feared losing by morning. “It’s my daughter Lotte-Lene I must discuss. She’s beautiful, confirmed, and I wish to see her settled.” “But I’m no widower!” chuckled the Councilor, “and have no son for her.” “Understand me, Councilor,” said the man. “She plays piano, sings; you must hear her upstairs. You know not all she can do; she can talk and entertain. She’s made for the stage, a good path for pretty girls of good families; they might marry a count, though neither I nor Lotte-Lene think that. She sings and plays, so I took her to singing school. She sang, but lacks a beer bass in women, nor shrieks those high canary notes now demanded, so they advised against that career. Well, I thought, if not a singer, an actress, needing only speech. Today I told the Instructor. ‘Is she well-read?’ he asked. ‘No,’ I said. ‘But an actress must be well-read!’ said he. She has time, I thought, and went home. She can go to a rental library and read what’s there.”

“But tonight, undressing, it struck me—why rent when one can borrow? The Councilor has plenty of books; let her read them; enough here gratis!” “Lotte-Lene is a nice girl,” said the Councilor, “a beauty! She shall have books. But has she grit, spirit, aptitude, genius? And equally, luck?” “She’s won the lottery twice,” said the grocer. “Once a clothes cabinet, once six pairs of bedsheets; that I call luck!” “I’ll ask the key,” said the Councilor. He placed the key on his right forefinger and the grocer’s, and it swung, giving letter after letter.

The key said, “Victory and luck!” So Lotte-Lene’s future was set. The Councilor gave her two books: Dyveke and Knigge’s Social Intercourse. That night began closer acquaintance between Lotte-Lene and the couple. She visited upstairs, and the Councilor found her sensible; she believed in him and the key. Mrs. Councilor saw childish innocence in her frank ignorance. Both were fond of her, each in their way, and she of them. “It smells lovely upstairs,” Lotte-Lene would say. The hallway held an apple fragrance from a barrel of graystone apples Mrs. Councilor stored; roses and lavender scented the rooms. “Something refined in that!” said Lotte-Lene. Her eyes delighted in the many flowers Mrs. Councilor kept, lilacs and cherry slips blooming even in winter. Leafless twigs cut and placed in water in the warm room soon leafed and flowered. “One would think life gone from these bare branches, but see how they rise from the dead. I never realized how wonderful nature is,” said Lotte-Lene. The Councilor showed her his “key book,” recording strange things the key had said—even about half an apple cake vanishing from the cupboard the evening the maid had her sweetheart over. The Councilor asked his key, “Who ate the apple cake, the cat or the sweetheart?” The key replied, “The sweetheart.” The Councilor had suspected so; the maid confessed. “That cursed key knows all!” “Yes, isn’t it strange!” said the Councilor. “That key! And of Lotte-Lene it said, ‘Victory and luck.’ We shall see! I swear.” “Wonderful,” said Lotte-Lene. Mrs. Councilor was less sure, but voiced no doubts before her husband. Later, she confided in Lotte-Lene that the Councilor, young, had been quite taken with theater. With a little push, he’d have become an actor, but his family pushed the opposite way. Still, he aspired to the stage and wrote a play. “This is a great secret, little Lotte-Lene. The play was not bad; accepted at the Royal Theater, then hissed out, and none have heard of it since, which gladdens me. I’m his wife and know him. Now you seek such a career too. I wish you all good, but I think things won’t work as predicted; I believe not in the gate key.” Lotte-Lene believed, uniting with the Councilor in that belief. Their hearts understood each other, in honor and chastity. The girl had many skills Mrs. Councilor valued: making starch from potatoes, silk gloves from old stockings, recovering silk dancing shoes, though she could afford new clothes. She had, as the grocer said, pennies in the table drawer and credit notes in her safe. She’d make a fine wife for the Pharmacist, thought Mrs. Councilor, but she said nothing and let not the key speak of it. The Pharmacist would soon settle with his own pharmacy in a nearby large provincial town.

Lotte-Lene read Dyveke and Knigge’s Social Intercourse for two years, memorizing Dyveke entirely—all parts, though she wished only to play Dyveke. She wanted not to debut in the capital, full of envy where they’d not have her anyway. She’d start her artistic career, as the Councilor called it, in a large provincial town—which, strangely, was where the youthful Pharmacist settled as the town’s youngest pharmacist. The long-awaited night came for Lotte-Lene’s debut and “victory and luck,” as the key said. The Councilor was absent, lying in bed, his wife nursing him with warm napkins and camomile tea—napkins about his body, tea within. While the couple missed the Dyveke performance, the Pharmacist attended, writing his relative, Mrs. Councilor, about it. “Dyveke’s ruff was the best,” he wrote. “Had I the Councilor’s gate key in my pocket, I’d have pulled it out as a whistle; she deserved it, and the key deserved it for its nasty lie of ‘victory and luck.’” The Councilor read the letter. It was spite, he said, key hatred toward an innocent girl. Once out of bed and himself again, he sent a short, poisonous note to the Pharmacist, who replied as if seeing only jest and good humor. He thanked him for any future contribution to revealing keys’ worth and significance; next, he confided that besides pharmacy, he was writing a great key novel where all characters were keys. A gate key, naturally central—patterned after the Councilor’s—was gifted with prophetic vision; around it revolved others: the old chamberlain’s key, versed in court splendor; the watch key, small, refined, worth few pennies; the church-pew key, counting itself clergy, seeing ghosts from a night in its keyhole; the larder, wine-cellar, and coal-cellar keys all appeared, bowing and turning around the gate key. Sunbeams brightened it to silver, and the wind, earth’s spirit, entered its body, making it whistle! It was key of all keys, the Councilor’s gate key, now key of the heavenly gate itself, the papal key, infallible! “Wickedness!” said the Councilor. “Great wickedness!” They never met again—save once, at Mrs. Councilor’s funeral. She died first. Sorrow and emptiness filled the house. Even cherry slips that had rooted and flowered seemed to mourn and fade, forgotten, for she tended them not. The Councilor and Pharmacist walked side by side behind her coffin, as nearest relations. This was no time for quarreling. Lotte-Lene tied mourning crape around the Councilor’s hat. She lived in the house again, having returned without victory or luck in her career. Yet that might still come; Lotte-Lene had a future; the key said so, and the Councilor said so. She went to him. They spoke of the departed and wept, for Lotte-Lene was tenderhearted; but discussing art, she felt strong. “Theater life is charming,” she said, “but full of nonsense and envy! I’d rather go my own way. Myself first, then art!” Knigge told truth in his actor chapter; she knew it; the key had not, but she never told the Councilor; she was fond of him. Besides, the gate key comforted him through the year of mourning. He asked it questions; it gave answers. When the year passed, he and Lotte-Lene sat together one inspiring evening; he asked the key, “Will I marry, and whom?” None pushed him, but he pushed the key, and it answered, “Lotte-Lene!” So it was said, and Lotte-Lene became Mrs. Councilor. “Victory and luck!” And these words had been said before—by the gate key.

text: There is nobody in the world who knows so many stories as Ole-Luk-Oie, or who can relate them so nicely. In the evening, while the children are seated at the table or in their little chairs, he comes up the stairs very softly, for he walks in his socks, then he opens the doors without the slightest noise, and throws a small quantity of very fine dust in their eyes, just enough to prevent them from keeping them open, and so they do not see him. Then he creeps behind them, and blows softly upon their necks, till their heads begin to droop. But Ole-Luk-Oie does not wish to hurt them, for he is very fond of children, and only wants them to be quiet that he may relate to them pretty stories, and they never are quiet until they are in bed and asleep. As soon as they are asleep, Ole-Luk-Oie seats himself upon the bed. He is nicely dressed; his coat is made of silken stuff; it is impossible to say of what color, for it changes from green to red, and from red to blue as he turns from side to side. Under each arm he carries an umbrella; one of them, with pictures on the inside, he spreads over the good children, and then they dream the most beautiful stories the whole night. But the other umbrella has no pictures, and this he holds over the naughty children so that they sleep heavily, and wake in the morning without having dreamed at all. Now we shall hear how Ole-Luk-Oie came every night during a whole week to the little boy named Hjalmar, and what he told him. There were seven stories, as there are seven days in the week. "Now pay attention," said Ole-Luk-Oie, in the evening, when Hjalmar was in bed, "and I will decorate the room." Immediately all the flowers in the flower-pots became large trees, with long branches reaching to the ceiling, and stretching along the walls, so that the whole room was like a greenhouse. All the branches were loaded with flowers, each flower as beautiful and as fragrant as a rose; and, had any one tasted them, he would have found them sweeter even than jam. The fruit glittered like gold, and there were cakes so full of plums that they were nearly bursting. It was incomparably beautiful. At the same time sounded dismal moans from the table-drawer in which lay Hjalmar's school books. "What can that be now?" said Ole-Luk-Oie, going to the table and pulling out the drawer. It was a slate, in such distress because of a false number in the sum, that it had almost broken itself to pieces. The pencil pulled and tugged at its string as if it were a little dog that wanted to help, but could not. And then came a moan from Hjalmar's copy-book. Oh, it was quite terrible to hear! On each leaf stood a row of capital letters, every one having a small letter by its side. This formed a copy; under these were other letters, which Hjalmar had written: they fancied they looked like the copy, but they were mistaken; for they were leaning on one side as if they intended to fall over the pencil-lines. "See, this is the way you should hold yourselves," said the copy. "Look here, you should slope thus, with a graceful curve." "Oh, we are very willing to do so, but we cannot," said Hjalmar's letters; "we are so wretchedly made." "You must be scratched out, then," said Ole-Luk-Oie. "Oh, no!" they cried, and then they stood up so gracefully it was quite a pleasure to look at them. "Now we must give up our stories, and exercise these letters," said Ole-Luk-Oie; "One, two--one, two--" So he drilled them till they stood up gracefully, and looked as beautiful as a copy could look. But after Ole-Luk-Oie was gone, and Hjalmar looked at them in the morning, they were as wretched and as awkward as ever. As soon as Hjalmar was in bed, Ole-Luk-Oie touched, with his little magic wand, all the furniture in the room, which immediately began to chatter, and each article only talked of itself. Over the chest of drawers hung a large picture in a gilt frame, representing a landscape, with fine old trees, flowers in the grass, and a broad stream, which flowed through the wood, past several castles, far out into the wild ocean. Ole-Luk-Oie touched the picture with his magic wand, and immediately the birds commenced singing, the branches of the trees rustled, and the clouds moved across the sky, casting their shadows on the landscape beneath them. Then Ole-Luk-Oie lifted little Hjalmar up to the frame, and placed his feet in the picture, just on the high grass, and there he stood with the sun shining down upon him through the branches of the trees. He ran to the water, and seated himself in a little boat which lay there, and which was painted red and white. The sails glittered like silver, and six swans, each with a golden circlet round its neck, and a bright blue star on its forehead, drew the boat past the green wood, where the trees talked of robbers and witches, and the flowers of beautiful little elves and fairies, whose histories the butterflies had related to them. Brilliant fish, with scales like silver and gold, swam after the boat, sometimes making a spring and splashing the water round them, while birds, red and blue, small and great, flew after him in two long lines. The gnats danced round them, and the cockchafers cried "Buz, buz." They all wanted to follow Hjalmar, and all had some story to tell him. It was a most pleasant sail. Sometimes the forests were thick and dark, sometimes like a beautiful garden, gay with sunshine and flowers; then he passed great palaces of glass and of marble, and on the balconies stood princesses, whose faces were those of little girls whom Hjalmar knew well, and had often played with. One of them held out her hand, in which was a heart made of sugar, more beautiful than any confectioner ever sold. As Hjalmar sailed by, he caught hold of one side of the sugar heart, and held it fast, and the princess held fast also, so that it broke in two pieces. Hjalmar had one piece, and the princess the other, but Hjalmar's was the largest. At each castle stood little princes acting as sentinels. They presented arms, and had golden swords, and made it rain plums and tin soldiers, so that they must have been real princes. Hjalmar continued to sail, sometimes through woods, sometimes as it were through large halls, and then by large cities. At last he came to the town where his nurse lived, who had carried him in her arms when he was a very little boy, and had always been kind to him. She nodded and beckoned to him, and then sang the little verses she had herself composed and set to him,-- "How oft my memory turns to thee, My own Hjalmar, ever dear! When I could watch thy infant glee, Or kiss away a pearly tear. 'Twas in my arms thy lisping tongue First spoke the half-remembered word, While o'er thy tottering steps I hung, My fond protection to afford. Farewell! I pray the Heavenly Power To keep thee till thy dying hour." And all the birds sang the same tune, the flowers danced on their stems, and the old trees nodded as if Ole-Luk-Oie had been telling them stories as well. How the rain did pour down! Hjalmar could hear it in his sleep; and when Ole-Luk-Oie opened the window, the water flowed quite up to the window-sill. It had the appearance of a large lake outside, and a beautiful ship lay close to the house. "Wilt thou sail with me to-night, little Hjalmar?" said Ole-Luk-Oie; "then we shall see foreign countries, and thou shalt return here in the morning." All in a moment, there stood Hjalmar, in his best clothes, on the deck of the noble ship; and immediately the weather became fine. They sailed through the streets, round by the church, and on every side rolled the wide, great sea. They sailed till the land disappeared, and then they saw a flock of storks, who had left their own country, and were travelling to warmer climates. The storks flew one behind the other, and had already been a long, long time on the wing. One of them seemed so tired that his wings could scarcely carry him. He was the last of the row, and was soon left very far behind. At length he sunk lower and lower, with outstretched wings, flapping them in vain, till his feet touched the rigging of the ship, and he slided from the sails to the deck, and stood before them. Then a sailor-boy caught him, and put him in the hen-house, with the fowls, the ducks, and the turkeys, while the poor stork stood quite bewildered amongst them. "Just look at that fellow," said the chickens. Then the turkey-cock puffed himself out as large as he could, and inquired who he was; and the ducks waddled backwards, crying, "Quack, quack." Then the stork told them all about warm Africa, of the pyramids, and of the ostrich, which, like a wild horse, runs across the desert. But the ducks did not understand what he said, and quacked amongst themselves, "We are all of the same opinion; namely, that he is stupid." "Yes, to be sure, he is stupid," said the turkey-cock; and gobbled. Then the stork remained quite silent, and thought of his home in Africa. "Those are handsome thin legs of yours," said the turkey-cock. "What do they cost a yard?" "Quack, quack, quack," grinned the ducks; but, the stork pretended not to hear. "You may as well laugh," said the turkey; "for that remark was rather witty, or perhaps it was above you. Ah, ah, is he not clever? He will be a great amusement to us while he remains here." And then he gobbled, and the ducks quacked, "Gobble, gobble; Quack, quack." What a terrible uproar they made, while they were having such fun among themselves! Then Hjalmar went to the hen-house; and, opening the door, called to the stork. Then he hopped out on the deck. He had rested himself now, and he looked happy, and seemed as if he nodded to Hjalmar, as if to thank him. Then he spread his wings, and flew away to warmer countries, while the hens clucked, the ducks quacked, and the turkey-cock turned quite scarlet in the head. "To-morrow you shall be made into soup," said Hjalmar to the fowls; and then he awoke, and found himself lying in his little bed. It was a wonderful journey which Ole-Luk-Oie had made him take this night. "What do you think I have got here?" said Ole-Luk-Oie, "Do not be frightened, and you shall see a little mouse." And then he held out his hand to him, in which lay a lovely little creature. "It has come to invite you to a wedding. Two little mice are going to enter into the marriage state tonight. They reside under the floor of your mother's store-room, and that must be a fine dwelling-place." "But how can I get through the little mouse-hole in the floor?" asked Hjalmar. "Leave me to manage that," said Ole-Luk-Oie. "I will soon make you small enough." And then he touched Hjalmar with his magic wand, whereupon he became less and less, until at last he was not longer than a little finger. "Now you can borrow the dress of the tin soldier. I think it will just fit you. It looks well to wear a uniform when you go into company." "Yes, certainly," said Hjalmar; and in a moment he was dressed as neatly as the neatest of all tin soldiers. "Will you be so good as to seat yourself in your mamma's thimble," said the little mouse, "that I may have the pleasure of drawing you to the wedding." "Will you really take so much trouble, young lady?" said Hjalmar. And so in this way he rode to the mouse's wedding. First they went under the floor, and then passed through a long passage, which was scarcely high enough to allow the thimble to drive under, and the whole passage was lit up with the phosphorescent light of rotten wood. "Does it not smell delicious?" asked the mouse, as she drew him along. "The wall and the floor have been smeared with bacon-rind; nothing can be nicer." Very soon they arrived at the bridal hall. On the right stood all the little lady-mice, whispering and giggling, as if they were making game of each other. To the left were the gentlemen-mice, stroking their whiskers with their fore-paws; and in the centre of the hall could be seen the bridal pair, standing side by side, in a hollow cheese-rind, and kissing each other, while all eyes were upon them; for they had already been betrothed, and were soon to be married. More and more friends kept arriving, till the mice were nearly treading each other to death; for the bridal pair now stood in the doorway, and none could pass in or out. The room had been rubbed over with bacon-rind, like the passage, which was all the refreshment offered to the guests. But for dessert they produced a pea, on which a mouse belonging to the bridal pair had bitten the first letters of their names. This was something quite uncommon. All the mice said it was a very beautiful wedding, and that they had been very agreeably entertained. After this, Hjalmar returned home. He had certainly been in grand society; but he had been obliged to creep under a room, and to make himself small enough to wear the uniform of a tin soldier. "It is incredible how many old people there are who would be glad to have me at night," said Ole-Luk-Oie, "especially those who have done something wrong. 'Good little Ole,' say they to me, 'we cannot close our eyes, and we lie awake the whole night and see all our evil deeds sitting on our beds like little imps, and sprinkling us with hot water. Will you come and drive them away, that we may have a good night's rest?' and then they sigh so deeply and say, 'We would gladly pay you for it. Good-night, Ole-Luk, the money lies on the window.' But I never do anything for gold." "What shall we do to-night?" asked Hjalmar. "I do not know whether you would care to go to another wedding," he replied, "although it is quite a different affair to the one we saw last night. Your sister's large doll, that is dressed like a man, and is called Herman, intends to marry the doll Bertha. It is also the dolls' birthday, and they will receive many presents." "Yes, I know that already," said Hjalmar, "my sister always allows her dolls to keep their birthdays or to have a wedding when they require new clothes; that has happened already a hundred times, I am quite sure." "Yes, so it may; but to-night is the hundred and first wedding, and when that has taken place it must be the last, therefore this is to be extremely beautiful. Only look." Hjalmar looked at the table, and there stood the little card-board doll's house, with lights in all the windows, and drawn up before it were the tin soldiers presenting arms. The bridal pair were seated on the floor, leaning against the leg of the table, looking very thoughtful, and with good reason. Then Ole-Luk-Oie dressed up in grandmother's black gown married them. As soon as the ceremony was concluded, all the furniture in the room joined in singing a beautiful song, which had been composed by the lead pencil, and which went to the melody of a military tattoo. "What merry sounds are on the wind, As marriage rites together bind A quiet and a loving pair, Though formed of kid, yet smooth and fair! Hurrah! If they are deaf and blind, We'll sing, though weather prove unkind." And now came the present; but the bridal pair had nothing to eat, for love was to be their food. "Shall we go to a country house, or travel?" asked the bridegroom. Then they consulted the swallow who had travelled so far, and the old hen in the yard, who had brought up five broods of chickens. And the swallow talked to them of warm countries, where the grapes hang in large clusters on the vines, and the air is soft and mild, and about the mountains glowing with colors more beautiful than we can think of. "But they have no red cabbage like we have," said the hen, "I was once in the country with my chickens for a whole summer, there was a large sand-pit, in which we could walk about and scratch as we liked. Then we got into a garden in which grew red cabbage; oh, how nice it was, I cannot think of anything more delicious." "But one cabbage stalk is exactly like another," said the swallow; "and here we have often bad weather." "Yes, but we are accustomed to it," said the hen. "But it is so cold here, and freezes sometimes." "Cold weather is good for cabbages," said the hen; "besides we do have it warm here sometimes. Four years ago, we had a summer that lasted more than five weeks, and it was so hot one could scarcely breathe. And then in this country we have no poisonous animals, and we are free from robbers. He must be wicked who does not consider our country the finest of all lands. He ought not to be allowed to live here." And then the hen wept very much and said, "I have also travelled. I once went twelve miles in a coop, and it was not pleasant travelling at all." "The hen is a sensible woman," said the doll Bertha. "I don't care for travelling over mountains, just to go up and come down again. No, let us go to the sand-pit in front of the gate, and then take a walk in the cabbage garden." And so they settled it. "Am I to hear any more stories?" asked little Hjalmar, as soon as Ole-Luk-Oie had sent him to sleep. "We shall have no time this evening," said he, spreading out his prettiest umbrella over the child. "Look at these Chinese," and then the whole umbrella appeared like a large china bowl, with blue trees and pointed bridges, upon which stood little Chinamen nodding their heads. "We must make all the world beautiful for to-morrow morning," said Ole-Luk-Oie, "for it will be a holiday, it is Sunday. I must now go to the church steeple and see if the little sprites who live there have polished the bells, so that they may sound sweetly. Then I must go into the fields and see if the wind has blown the dust from the grass and the leaves, and the most difficult task of all which I have to do, is to take down all the stars and brighten them up. I have to number them first before I put them in my apron, and also to number the places from which I take them, so that they may go back into the right holes, or else they would not remain, and we should have a number of falling stars, for they would all tumble down one after the other." "Hark ye! Mr. Luk-Oie," said an old portrait which hung on the wall of Hjalmar's bedroom. "Do you know me? I am Hjalmar's great-grandfather. I thank you for telling the boy stories, but you must not confuse his ideas. The stars cannot be taken down from the sky and polished; they are spheres like our earth, which is a good thing for them." "Thank you, old great-grandfather," said Ole-Luk-Oie. "I thank you; you may be the head of the family, as no doubt you are, but I am older than you. I am an ancient heathen. The old Romans and Greeks named me the Dream-god. I have visited the noblest houses, and continue to do so; still I know how to conduct myself both to high and low, and now you may tell the stories yourself:" and so Ole-Luk-Oie walked off, taking his umbrellas with him. "Well, well, one is never to give an opinion, I suppose," grumbled the portrait. And it woke Hjalmar. "Good evening," said Ole-Luk-Oie. Hjalmar nodded, and then sprang out of bed, and turned his great-grandfather's portrait to the wall, so that it might not interrupt them as it had done yesterday. "Now," said he, "you must tell me some stories about five green peas that lived in one pod; or of the chickseed that courted the chickweed; or of the darning needle, who acted so proudly because she fancied herself an embroidery needle." "You may have too much of a good thing," said Ole-Luk-Oie. "You know that I like best to show you something, so I will show you my brother. He is also called Ole-Luk-Oie but he never visits any one but once, and when he does come, he takes him away on his horse, and tells him stories as they ride along. He knows only two stories. One of these is so wonderfully beautiful, that no one in the world can imagine anything at all like it; but the other is just as ugly and frightful, so that it would be impossible to describe it." Then Ole-Luk-Oie lifted Hjalmar up to the window. "There now, you can see my brother, the other Ole-Luk-Oie; he is also called Death. You perceive he is not so bad as they represent him in picture books; there he is a skeleton, but now his coat is embroidered with silver, and he wears the splendid uniform of a hussar, and a mantle of black velvet flies behind him, over the horse. Look, how he gallops along." Hjalmar saw that as this Ole-Luk-Oie rode on, he lifted up old and young, and carried them away on his horse. Some he seated in front of him, and some behind, but always inquired first, "How stands the mark-book?" "Good," they all answered. "Yes, but let me see for myself," he replied; and they were obliged to give him the books. Then all those who had "Very good," or "Exceedingly good," came in front of the horse, and heard the beautiful story; while those who had "Middling," or "Tolerably good," in their books, were obliged to sit behind, and listen to the frightful tale. They trembled and cried, and wanted to jump down from the horse, but they could not get free, for they seemed fastened to the seat. "Why, Death is a most splendid Luk-Oie," said Hjalmar. "I am not in the least afraid of him." "You need have no fear of him," said Ole-Luk-Oie, "if you take care and keep a good conduct book." "Now I call that very instructive," murmured the great-grandfather's portrait. "It is useful sometimes to express an opinion;" so he was quite satisfied. These are some of the doings and sayings of Ole-Luk-Oie. I hope he may visit you himself this evening, and relate some more.
rewrite: No one in the world knows as many tales as Ole-Luk-Oie, and none can tell them so delightfully. In the evening, when the children sit at the table or on their stools, he softly ascends the stairs, for he walks in stockinged feet, then he noiselessly opens the door, sprinkles a tiny bit of fine dust into their eyes—just enough to keep them from staying open—so they do not see him. He then slips behind them and breathes gently on their necks until their heads begin to nod. But Ole-Luk-Oie means no harm; he is very fond of children and only wants them to be still so he can tell them lovely stories, and they are never quiet until they are in bed and asleep. As soon as they sleep, Ole-Luk-Oie sits on the bed. He is finely dressed; his coat is of silk, but it is impossible to say what color, for it shifts from green to red and from red to blue as he turns. Under each arm he carries an umbrella; one, with pictures inside, he spreads over good children, and they dream the most beautiful tales all night. The other umbrella has no pictures, and this he holds over naughty children so they sleep heavily and wake in the morning without any dreams. Now we shall hear how Ole-Luk-Oie visited a little boy named Hjalmar every night for a whole week and what he told him. There were seven stories, as there are seven days in the week. "Now pay attention," said Ole-Luk-Oie one evening when Hjalmar was in bed, "and I will decorate the room." Instantly, all the flowers in the pots grew into large trees, their long branches reaching to the ceiling and along the walls, making the room like a greenhouse. The branches were laden with flowers, each as lovely and fragrant as a rose; had anyone tasted them, they would have found them sweeter than jam. The fruit glittered like gold, and there were cakes so stuffed with plums they nearly burst. It was incomparably beautiful. At the same time, mournful groans came from the table drawer where Hjalmar’s schoolbooks lay. "What can that be?" said Ole-Luk-Oie, going to the table and pulling out the drawer. It was a slate, so distressed over a wrong number in a sum that it had almost shattered itself. The pencil tugged at its string like a little dog wanting to help but unable to. Then came a moan from Hjalmar’s copybook. Oh, it was quite dreadful to hear! On each page stood a row of capital letters, each with a small letter beside it, forming a copy; below these were other letters Hjalmar had written: they fancied they resembled the copy, but they were mistaken, for they leaned as if about to topple off the lines. "See, this is how you should hold yourselves," said the copy. "Look, you should slope with a graceful curve." "Oh, we wish we could, but we cannot," said Hjalmar’s letters; "we are so poorly made." "Then you must be scratched out," said Ole-Luk-Oie. "Oh, no!" they cried, and then they stood up so gracefully it was a pleasure to behold. "Now we must pause our stories and drill these letters," said Ole-Luk-Oie; "One, two—one, two—" So he drilled them until they stood gracefully, looking as fine as any copy. But after Ole-Luk-Oie left and Hjalmar looked at them in the morning, they were as wretched and awkward as ever. Once Hjalmar was in bed, Ole-Luk-Oie touched all the furniture with his little magic wand, and immediately everything began to chatter, each piece speaking only of itself. Over the chest of drawers hung a large picture in a gilt frame, showing a landscape with grand old trees, flowers in the grass, and a broad stream flowing through the woods, past castles, far out to the wild ocean. Ole-Luk-Oie touched the picture with his wand, and at once the birds sang, the tree branches rustled, and clouds drifted across the sky, casting shadows below. Then Ole-Luk-Oie lifted little Hjalmar to the frame and set his feet in the picture, right on the tall grass, where he stood with sunlight filtering through the trees. He ran to the water and sat in a little boat painted red and white that lay there. The sails gleamed like silver, and six swans, each with a golden circlet around its neck and a bright blue star on its forehead, drew the boat past the green woods, where trees spoke of robbers and witches, and flowers told of tiny elves and fairies, whose histories butterflies had shared. Brilliant fish with silver and gold scales swam after the boat, sometimes leaping and splashing, while birds of red and blue, small and large, flew after him in two long lines. Gnats danced around, and cockchafers buzzed. They all wished to follow Hjalmar, each with a story to tell. It was a delightful sail. Sometimes the forests were dense and dark, sometimes like a sunny garden bright with flowers; then he passed great palaces of glass and marble, with princesses on the balconies—faces of little girls Hjalmar knew well and often played with. One held out her hand with a sugar heart lovelier than any confectioner’s. As Hjalmar sailed by, he grasped one side, and the princess held the other, so it broke in two. Hjalmar got the larger piece. At each castle stood little prince sentinels presenting arms, with golden swords, making it rain plums and tin soldiers—they must have been real princes. Hjalmar sailed on, through woods, through great halls, then by large cities. At last he reached the town where his old nurse lived, who had carried him in her arms as a toddler and always been kind. She nodded and beckoned, then sang verses she had composed for him: "How oft my memory turns to thee, My own Hjalmar, ever dear! When I could watch thy infant glee, Or kiss away a pearly tear. 'Twas in my arms thy lisping tongue First spoke the half-remembered word, While o'er thy tottering steps I hung, My fond protection to afford. Farewell! I pray the Heavenly Power To keep thee till thy dying hour." And all the birds sang the same tune, flowers danced on their stems, and old trees nodded as if Ole-Luk-Oie had been telling them stories too. How the rain poured down! Hjalmar heard it in his sleep; and when Ole-Luk-Oie opened the window, water rose to the sill. Outside it looked like a vast lake, with a beautiful ship near the house. "Will you sail with me tonight, little Hjalmar?" said Ole-Luk-Oie; "then we shall see foreign lands, and you shall return by morning." In an instant, Hjalmar stood in his best clothes on the deck of the noble ship; and the weather cleared at once. They sailed through streets, past the church, and on every side rolled the wide, great sea. They sailed until land vanished, then saw a flock of storks migrating to warmer climates. They flew in a line, having been airborne a long while. One seemed so weary his wings could barely carry him. He lagged last, falling far behind. He sank lower, wings flapping vainly, until his feet touched the ship’s rigging, and he slid from the sails to the deck, standing before them. A cabin boy caught him and put him in the hen-house with chickens, ducks, and turkeys, while the poor stork stood bewildered. "Just look at that fellow," said the chickens. The turkey puffed himself up and asked who he was; the ducks waddled back, quacking. The stork told of warm Africa, pyramids, and ostriches racing across deserts. But the ducks didn’t understand and quacked among themselves, "We all agree he is stupid." "Yes, certainly, he is stupid," said the turkey-cock, gobbling. The stork fell silent, thinking of his African home. "Those are fine thin legs of yours," said the turkey-cock. "What do they cost a yard?" "Quack, quack, quack," grinned the ducks; but the stork pretended not to hear. "You may as well laugh," said the turkey; "for that was rather witty, or perhaps beyond you. Ah, isn’t he clever? He’ll amuse us while he’s here." And he gobbled, and the ducks quacked, "Gobble, gobble; Quack, quack." What a terrible uproar they made, amusing themselves! Then Hjalmar went to the hen-house, opened the door, and called the stork. He hopped onto the deck, rested now, looking happy, and seemed to nod thanks to Hjalmar. Then he spread his wings and flew to warmer countries, while hens clucked, ducks quacked, and the turkey-cock’s head turned scarlet. "Tomorrow you shall be soup," said Hjalmar to the fowls; then he awoke in his little bed. It was a wondrous journey Ole-Luk-Oie had taken him on that night. "Guess what I have here?" said Ole-Luk-Oie, "Don’t be scared, and you’ll see a little mouse." He held out his hand with a lovely little creature. "It has come to invite you to a wedding. Two little mice marry tonight. They live under your mother’s storeroom floor, which must be a fine home." "But how can I get through the mouse-hole?" asked Hjalmar. "Leave that to me," said Ole-Luk-Oie. "I’ll soon make you small enough." He touched Hjalmar with his magic wand, and he shrank until no longer than a finger. "Now you can borrow the tin soldier’s uniform. It should fit. It looks well to wear uniform in company." "Yes, certainly," said Hjalmar; and instantly he was dressed as neatly as the smartest tin soldier. "Please sit in your mama’s thimble," said the little mouse, "so I may have the pleasure of pulling you to the wedding." "Will you really take such trouble, young lady?" said Hjalmar. And so he rode to the mouse wedding. First under the floor, then through a long passage barely high enough for the thimble, lit by phosphorescent rotten wood. "Doesn’t it smell delicious?" asked the mouse, pulling him along. "The wall and floor are smeared with bacon-rind; nothing nicer." Soon they reached the bridal hall. On the right stood lady-mice, whispering and giggling; on the left, gentlemen-mice stroking whiskers with fore-paws; in the center stood the bridal pair in a hollow cheese-rind, kissing, all eyes on them, for they were betrothed and soon to marry. More friends arrived until mice nearly trampled each other; the pair stood in the doorway, blocking passage. The room, like the passage, was rubbed with bacon-rind—the only refreshment. For dessert, they produced a pea on which a mouse of the pair had bitten their initials. This was quite uncommon. All said it was a beautiful wedding and they were agreeably entertained. After, Hjalmar returned home. He had been in grand society but had to creep under a room and shrink to wear a tin soldier’s uniform. "It’s incredible how many old people wish for me at night," said Ole-Luk-Oie, "especially those who’ve done wrong. ‘Good little Ole,’ they say, ‘we cannot close our eyes; we lie awake all night seeing our misdeeds like imps on our beds, sprinkling us with hot water. Will you drive them away so we may rest?’ and they sigh, ‘We’d gladly pay. Good-night, Ole-Luk, the money is on the window.’ But I never do anything for gold." "What shall we do tonight?" asked Hjalmar. "I don’t know if you’d like another wedding," he replied, "though quite different from last night’s. Your sister’s large doll, dressed as a man named Herman, intends to marry doll Bertha. It’s also the dolls’ birthday, and they’ll get many presents." "Yes, I know," said Hjalmar, "my sister lets her dolls have birthdays or weddings when they need new clothes; that’s happened a hundred times, I’m sure." "Yes, but tonight is the hundred and first wedding, and after that it must be the last, so this will be extremely beautiful. Just look." Hjalmar looked at the table, and there stood the little cardboard doll’s house, lights in every window, with tin soldiers presenting arms before it. The bridal pair sat on the floor, leaning against a table leg, looking thoughtful, and with good reason. Then Ole-Luk-Oie, dressed in grandmother’s black gown, married them. Once the ceremony ended, all furniture sang a lovely song composed by the lead pencil to a military tune: "What merry sounds are on the wind, As marriage rites together bind A quiet and a loving pair, Though formed of kid, yet smooth and fair! Hurrah! If they are deaf and blind, We’ll sing, though weather prove unkind." Then came presents; but the pair had nothing to eat, for love was their food. "Shall we go to a country house or travel?" asked the groom. They consulted the well-traveled swallow and the old yard hen who had raised five broods. The swallow spoke of warm lands where grapes hang in clusters, the air is soft, and mountains glow with beautiful colors. "But they have no red cabbage like ours," said the hen, "I once spent a whole summer in the country with my chicks; there was a large sand-pit where we could scratch about. Then we got into a garden with red cabbage; oh, how nice, I can’t think of anything more delicious." "But one cabbage stalk is like another," said the swallow; "and here we often have bad weather." "Yes, but we’re used to it," said the hen. "But it’s so cold here, and sometimes freezes." "Cold weather is good for cabbages," said the hen; "besides, we do have warm times. Four years ago, summer lasted over five weeks, so hot one could scarcely breathe. And here we have no poisonous animals or robbers. He must be wicked who doesn’t think our land finest. He shouldn’t be allowed to live here." Then the hen wept and said, "I’ve also travelled. I once went twelve miles in a coop, and it wasn’t pleasant at all." "The hen is sensible," said doll Bertha. "I don’t care for travelling over mountains, just up and down. No, let’s go to the sand-pit by the gate and walk in the cabbage garden." And so they settled it. "Am I to hear more stories?" asked little Hjalmar, once Ole-Luk-Oie had sent him to sleep. "We’ll have no time tonight," said he, spreading his prettiest umbrella over the child. "Look at these Chinese," and the whole umbrella looked like a large china bowl with blue trees and pointed bridges, little Chinamen nodding. "We must make the world beautiful for tomorrow morning," said Ole-Luk-Oie, "for it’s a holiday, Sunday. I must go to the church steeple to see if sprites have polished the bells to sound sweetly. Then to the fields to see if wind has blown dust from grass and leaves, and my hardest task: take down all stars and brighten them. I number them before putting them in my apron, and number their places so they return to the right holes, or else they wouldn’t stay, and we’d have falling stars tumbling down." "Hark, Mr. Luk-Oie," said an old portrait on Hjalmar’s wall. "Do you know me? I am Hjalmar’s great-grandfather. I thank you for telling the boy stories, but you mustn’t confuse him. Stars can’t be taken down and polished; they are spheres like our earth, which is good." "Thank you, old great-grandfather," said Ole-Luk-Oie. "You may be family head, but I am older. I am an ancient heathen. Romans and Greeks named me Dream-god. I’ve visited noblest houses and still do; I know how to conduct myself with high and low. Now you may tell stories yourself:" and Ole-Luk-Oie walked off with his umbrellas. "Well, one is never to give an opinion, I suppose," grumbled the portrait. And it woke Hjalmar. "Good evening," said Ole-Luk-Oie. Hjalmar nodded, sprang out of bed, and turned his great-grandfather’s portrait to the wall so it wouldn’t interrupt as yesterday. "Now," said he, "tell me stories about five green peas in one pod; or chickseed courting chickweed; or the darning needle who acted proud thinking herself an embroidery needle."
