When the wind passes over the grass, the blades sway like lake water; over the cornfield, the ears curl into waves like those on a lake—this is the Wind’s dance. But listen as he tells the tale; he sings it aloud; and how different his melody among the forest trees is from his shriek through cracks and crevices in old walls. Watch him chase fleecy white clouds across the sky like a flock of sheep; hear him howl through the open gate, as if he were a watchman blowing his horn. Oddly, he whistles down the chimney until the hearth fire blazes below, and it is cozy to sit in the warm room and listen to stories. Let the Wind himself be the storyteller! He knows more wondrous tales than all of us combined. Hear how he begins: “Whew, whew, whew! On, on, on!” That is the refrain of his song.

“By the Great Belt stands an old manor with thick red walls,” says the Wind. “I know every stone; I knew them when they were part of Marsk Stig’s castle on the cliff. They were torn down and rebuilt into a new wall and a new house—Borreby Manor, which still stands. I have seen and known all the noble folk of various families who lived there. Now I shall tell of Valdemar Daae and his daughters.

“He was a proud man, of royal blood. He knew more than hunting stags or draining a cup. ‘All will turn out well,’ he would say.

“His noble wife stepped lightly in cloth-of-gold over polished mosaic floors. Splendid tapestries and costly carved furniture surrounded her; she brought silver and gold into the house; German beer filled the cellar; proud black horses neighed in the stables. Ah, Borreby was then a home of wealth. And there were children—three fair daughters: Ide, Johanne, and Anna Dorothea. They were rich, noble, raised in luxury. Whew, whew, whew! On, on, on!” sang the Wind, then went on.

“Here I never saw, as in other old houses, the lady spinning among her maidens in the hall. She played the lute and sang, though not always Danish songs but foreign ones. There was life and merriment; distinguished guests came from near and far; music and clinking glasses were so loud even I could not drown them. There was pride here, boasting and bragging, and talk of power, but not the Lord’s blessings!

“Then one May day,” said the Wind, “I came from the west. I had seen ships wrecked on West Jutland’s coast, swept over heath and wooded shore to Funen, and now I crossed the Great Belt, blowing and roaring. I rested on Zealand’s coast, near Borreby, where the fine oak forest still grew. Young lads gathered the largest, driest branches; they carried them to town, piled them, set them ablaze, and youths and maidens sang and danced around.

“I lay still,” said the Wind, “but gently touched a branch brought by the handsomest lad, and his pile blazed highest. That made him leader, with first choice of a May lamb. There was joy, merriment, such as I never found in rich Borreby.

“Then a gilded carriage drawn by six horses approached, bearing the noble lady and her three daughters—so young, so fair—three sweet blossoms: a rose, a lily, a pale hyacinth. Their mother was a proud, splendid tulip; she offered no greeting to the peasants, who stopped their game and bowed; stiff as a tulip she held herself. Yes, rose, lily, and pale hyacinth—I saw them all; whose May lambs would they become? Surely their suitors would be proud knights, perhaps princes! Whew, whew, whew! On, on, on!

“The carriage rattled past, and the peasants resumed their dance. Summer was celebrated from town to town, in Borreby, Tjaereby, and all around.

“But when I rose that night, the highborn lady had lain down, never to rise again. That which comes to all had come to her; nothing new. Valdemar Daae stood grave and thoughtful; he seemed to say, ‘The proudest tree may bend, not break.’ The daughters wept; all eyes in the manor were dried. Lady Daae had passed—and I passed on! Whew, whew, whew!

“I returned, as I often crossed Funen and the Belt, resting near Borreby in the shelter of the oak forest. Here ospreys, wood pigeons, blue ravens, even black storks built nests; it was spring, some had eggs, some young. How they flew! How they cried! The sound of axes echoed, stroke after stroke; trees were to be felled. Valdemar Daae had decided to build a great three-deck warship, which the king would surely buy, so the trees must fall and birds lose homes. The hawk fled in terror as his nest was destroyed; osprey and others flew in anger, screaming wrath and agony; I understood them well. Crows and jackdaws shrieked scornfully, ‘Caw, caw! From the nests!’

“In the forest, with workmen, stood Valdemar Daae and his three daughters, laughing at the birds’ protests—all but the youngest, Anna Dorothea. Tenderhearted, when an old half-dead tree with a black stork’s nest was to be cut, she wept to see the helpless young thrusting their heads out, and begged it be spared. So the tree was left standing.

“There was much hammering and sawing as the three-deck ship was built. The master shipbuilder was a fine-looking young fellow, of low birth, eyes sparkling, brow thoughtful. Valdemar Daae liked to hear him talk, and so did little Ide, his eldest, now fifteen. While building the ship, he built castles in the air, seeing himself and Ide as man and wife. That might have happened if the castle were of stone, with ramparts, moat, forest, and gardens. But with all his skill, he was a common bird; what business had a sparrow among cranes? Whew, whew, whew! I flew away, he flew away, and little Ide forgot, as she must.

“In the stable, the beautiful black horses neighed. They were worth seeing, and were seen. The admiral, sent by the king to inspect the warship and discuss buying it, admired the splendid horses. I heard him,” said the Wind. “I followed the gentlemen through the open stable door, scattering wisps of straw, yellow as gold, about their feet. Gold! That was what Valdemar Daae wanted, and the admiral wanted the black horses, but their discussion came to nothing. Neither horses nor ship were bought! It lay on shore with planks over it, a Noah’s ark never to float. Whew, whew, whew! A pity!

“In winter, when fields were covered with snow and ice choked the Belt,” said the Wind, “flocks of black ravens and crows perched on the lifeless, solitary ship on shore. Frantic old birds and homeless young screamed hoarse tales of the ravaged oak forest and destroyed nests, all for this useless lumber, the proud vessel never to sail. I tossed snow about until it lay thick over the ship; I made it listen to my voice, taught it what a storm says; I did my part teaching it a ship’s knowledge. Whew, whew, whew! On, on, on!

“Winter passed, winter and summer passed, as they always pass, as I pass, as snow melts, leaves drift down, apple blossoms fade—away, away, away! And as people pass away!

“But the daughters were still young. Little Ide was as blooming a rose as when the shipbuilder saw her. Often I caught her long brown hair as she stood thoughtfully by the apple tree in the garden, not noticing I shook petals down, loosening it, as she gazed at the crimson sunset and golden sky through dark bushes. Her sister Johanne was like a lily, bright, slender, straight, stiff upon her stalk as her mother had been. She lingered in the great hall where ancestors’ portraits hung; ladies in velvet and silk, with pearl-embroidered hats on braids; beautiful indeed; men in steel armor, or stiff white ruffs and rich mantles lined with squirrel fur, swords at their sides. Johanne wondered how her portrait would look there, and what her husband would be. Yes, she thought and talked of it. I heard as I whipped through the long gallery into the hall and whirled around.

“Anna Dorothea, the pale hyacinth, was a quiet child of fourteen, with large, thoughtful blue eyes, and a child’s smile lingering on her lips. Even if I could, I would never blow that smile away. I met her in the garden, lane, or fields, gathering herbs and flowers for her father’s wondrous potions.

“Valdemar Daae, haughty and conceited, was also skilled and knowledgeable. People knew and spoke of it. Fire burned summer and winter in his study fireplace; his door was always locked; night and day he worked, yet seldom spoke of his labors. He knew nature’s secrets must be wooed secretly, and he sought the best—how to make pure red gold!

“Smoke rose continuously from the chimney, fire crackled. I was there!” sang the Wind. “I whistled up the chimney. ‘Stop it! Stop it!’ I sang. ‘It will end in smoke, dust, embers, ashes! You will burn up! Whew, whew! Stop!’ But Valdemar Daae did not stop.

“Those superb horses in the stable—what became of them? The fine old gold and silver in cupboards, cattle in meadows, the mansion and all its riches? All melted in the gold-making crucible, yet no gold came. Barn, granary, cellar, pantry—all empty; fewer folk, more mice. One pane broken, another cracked,” said the Wind, “and I no longer needed the door to enter. The chimney still smoked, not for cooking dinner, but for cooking red gold.

“I blew through courtyard gates like a watchman’s horn, but no watchman was there,” said the Wind. “I whirled the weathercock round; it creaked like a watchman’s snore, but there was none; only rats and mice; poverty loaded the table, stuffed wardrobe and larder; doors sagged; chinks and cracks let me come and go at will.

“In smoke and ashes, beset by sorrow and sleepless nights, Valdemar’s hair and beard turned gray, skin coarse and yellowish; eyes still greedily sought gold—the long-hoped-for gold!

“I blew ashes and smoke into his face and beard. I whistled through broken panes and cracks, blew into the daughters’ chest of drawers, where clothes, faded and threadbare from constant use, had to last. The poor dears never had such a song sung at their cradles; but none, save I, sang in the great hall now. Abundance had turned to poverty,” said the Wind. “I snowed them in; snow is said to cheer. They had no firewood, for the forest was destroyed. A sharp frost came; while I sprang through holes and passages, over walls and roofs to keep warm, the highborn daughters huddled in bed against the cold, their father beneath rude skins. Nothing to eat, nothing to burn!

“A hard lesson to learn!

“Whew, whew, whew! But Valdemar Daae couldn’t learn. ‘After winter comes spring,’ he said, ‘after troubles, good times; we must wait, wait! Now the mansion is mortgaged! High time indeed—and we shall have gold! By Easter!’ Then I saw him watch a spider at work, heard him mutter, ‘Good, industrious weaver, you teach perseverance! Your web may break, but you begin again; again torn, undismayed you return, and are rewarded at last!’

“Easter morning came, bells rang, sun shone. He awoke feverish; he had boiled, seethed, distilled, compounded. I heard him sigh like a lost soul, heard him pray; I felt him hold his breath. The lamp had gone out, but he did not notice. I blew on coals until a flame shone on his chalk-white face, lighting staring eyes. But those eyes grew larger—until they seemed about to burst.

“Behold the alchemistic glass! It glittered, glowing, pure and heavy; he lifted it with faltering hand; cried with stumbling tongue, ‘Gold! Gold!’ He staggered, dizzy; I could have blown him down,” said the Wind, “but I only blew on live coals, followed him to where his daughters sat, shivering. Ashes sprinkled his beard, clung to his dress, lay in matted hair. He stood erect, lifted high his treasure in fragile glass. ‘I’ve found it! I’ve won!’ he cried. ‘Gold!’ The glass flashed in sunbeams as he held it high—and then, lo! his hand trembled so the alchemistic glass fell, shattering into a thousand fragments! His last bubble burst! Whew, whew, whew! On, on, on! And I went on, away from the alchemist’s home.

“Toward year’s end, during short days when mist flings wet drops on red berries and leafless branches, I returned in happy spirits, swept heavens clean, broke off dead branches; not hard work, but it must be done. And at the same time, a different sweeping and cleaning occurred at Borreby. Valdemar Daae’s old enemy, Ove Ramel of Basnaes, was there with the mortgage on mansion and contents. I drummed on broken panes, beat against ruined doors, whistled through cracks; Master Ove shouldn’t find it pleasant. Ide and Anna Dorothea wept quietly; Johanne stood pale and stately, biting her thumb till it bled; but all did no good.

“Ove Ramel offered to let Mr. Daae remain at the mansion during his lifetime, but got no thanks. I listened, noticed how the homeless old nobleman held his head more proudly than ever. I rushed against mansion and old lime trees, so the thickest branch broke off—not a rotten one. It lay at the gate, like a broom for sweeping out—and there was sweeping out, you may be sure! But I had expected it.

“Oh, a day of bitterness—a sorrowful day! But with stiff neck and stout back, the proud man bore his burden bravely.

“They had nothing left but the clothes they wore, and the new alchemistic glass, filled with brittle treasure that promised so much—fool’s gold scraped from the floor; this Valdemar Daae hid in his breast. He took his cane, and with his three daughters, the once-rich nobleman walked out of Borreby. I blew cold upon his flaming cheeks, stroked his gray beard and long white hair to and fro as I sang loudly, ‘Whew, whew, whew! This was the end of his glory!’

“Ide and Anna Dorothea walked on each side; as Johanne crossed the threshold, she turned back. Perhaps, as he gazed wistfully at red stones that once made Marsk Stig’s castle, she remembered the old ballad:

The elder took the younger by the hand,
And forth they went to a distant land.

“Was she thinking of this? Here were three daughters, and their father with them. They turned from the highway, where they had driven in carriage, to Smidstrup Field, to a little mud shack rented for ten marks a year. These bare walls and empty chambers were their new ‘mansion.’ Crows and jackdaws circled above, screaming mockingly, ‘Turned out of the nest! Caw, Caw!’ as they had in Borreby Wood when oaks were cut down. Mr. Daae and his daughters must have understood; not pleasant to hear, so I did my best to drown them by blowing about their ears.

“Thus they passed into the mud shack on Smidstrup Field, and I passed away over field and moor, through bare hedges and leafless woods, over open waters to other lands—whew, whew! On, on! Year after year!”

What happened to Valdemar Daae; what happened to his daughters? The Wind will tell:

“The last time I saw them, I found only Anna Dorothea, the pale hyacinth. She was old and bent; half a century later. She had lived longest; she knew the whole story.

“Across the heath, near Viborg, stood the dean’s beautiful new house, with red stones, pointed gables, chimneys always smoking busily. The gentle lady and her beautiful daughters sat on the balcony, looking over hanging buckthorn in the garden to the brown heath; what did they look at? They looked at the stork’s nest on that dilapidated cottage. Houseleek and moss made most of the roof, if one could call it a roof; the stork’s nest covered the greater part, alone in good condition, for the stork kept it so.

“A house to look at but not touch,” said the Wind. “I passed gently. The hut remained only for the stork’s nest, for it was no credit to the heath. The dean didn’t want to drive the stork away, so the poor old woman who lived there had permission to stay and shelter as well as she could. For that she owed thanks to the queer Egyptian bird; or was it because, years ago, she had pleaded for the nest of his wild black brother in Borreby Wood? Then she, the poor woman, was a happy child, a delicate, pale hyacinth in her ancestral garden. She remembered now; Anna Dorothea forgot nothing.

“‘Oh!’ she sighed—humans can sigh almost like the Wind among reeds. ‘Oh!—no bells rang at your funeral, Valdemar Daae! No poor schoolboys sang psalms when Borreby’s former master was laid to rest! Oh, but everything ends—misery as well as happiness! It grieved my father worst that my sister Ide should become a peasant’s wife, a miserable peasant he could have punished by making him ride a hard plank. But he is at peace in the grave now, and you are with him, Ide! Oh, yes, ah, me—I am still here. I am old and poor. Deliver me, kind Christ!’

“Such was Anna Dorothea’s prayer in the miserable mud hut allowed to stand only for the stork.

text: When the wind sweeps across a field of grass it makes little ripples in it like a lake; in a field of corn it makes great waves like the sea itself: this is the wind's frolic. Then listen to the stories it tells; it sings them aloud, one kind of song among the trees of the forest, and a very different one when it is pent up within walls with all their cracks and crannies. Do you see how the wind chases the white fleecy clouds as if they were a flock of sheep? Do you hear the wind down there, howling in the open doorway like a watchman winding his horn? Then, too, how he whistles in the chimneys, making the fire crackle and sparkle. How cosy it is to sit in the warm glow of the fire listening to the tales it has to tell! Let the wind tell its own story! It can tell you more adventures than all of us put together. Listen now:-- 'Whew!--Whew!--Fare away!' That was the refrain of his song. 'Close to the Great Belt stands an old mansion with thick red walls,' says the wind. 'I know every stone of it; I knew them before when they formed part of Marsk Stig's Castle on the Ness. It had to come down. The stones were used again, and made a new wall of a new castle in another place--Borreby Hall as it now stands. 'I have watched the highborn men and women of all the various races who have lived there, and now I am going to tell you about Waldemar Daa and his daughters! 'He held his head very high, for he came of a royal stock! He knew more than the mere chasing of a stag, or the emptying of a flagon; he knew how to manage his affairs, he said himself. 'His lady wife walked proudly across the brightly polished floors, in her gold brocaded kirtle; the tapestries in the rooms were gorgeous, and the furniture of costly carved woods. She had brought much gold and silver plate into the house with her, and the cellars were full of German ale, when there was anything there at all. Fiery black horses neighed in the stables; Borreby Hall was a very rich place when wealth came there. 'Then there were the children, three dainty maidens, Ida, Johanna and Anna Dorothea. I remember their names well. 'They were rich and aristocratic people, and they were born and bred in wealth! Whew!--whew!--fare away!' roared the wind, then he went on with his story. 'I did not see here, as in other old noble castles the highborn lady sitting among her maidens in the great hall turning the spinning-wheel. No, she played upon the ringing lute, and sang to its tones. Her songs were not always the old Danish ditties, however, but songs in foreign tongues. All was life and hospitality; noble guests came from far and wide; there were sounds of music and the clanging of flagons, so loud that I could not drown them!' said the wind. 'Here were arrogance and ostentation enough and to spare; plenty of lords, but the Lord had no place there. 'Then came the evening of May-day!' said the wind. 'I came from the west; I had been watching ships being wrecked and broken up on the west coast of Jutland. I tore over the heaths and the green wooded coasts, across the island of Funen and over the Great Belt puffing and blowing. I settled down to rest on the coast of Zealand close to Borreby Hall, where the splendid forest of oaks still stood. The young bachelors of the neighbourhood came out and collected faggots and branches, the longest and driest they could find. These they took to the town, piled them up in a heap, and set fire to them; then the men and maidens danced and sang round the bonfire. I lay still,' said the wind, 'but I softly moved a branch, the one laid by the handsomest young man, and his billet blazed up highest of all. He was the chosen one, he had the name of honour, he became 'Buck of the Street!' and he chose from among the girls his little May-lamb. All was life and merriment, greater far than within rich Borreby Hall. 'The great lady came driving towards the Hall, in her gilded chariot drawn by six horses. She had her three dainty daughters with her; they were indeed three lovely flowers. A rose, a lily and a pale hyacinth. The mother herself was a gorgeous tulip; she took no notice whatever of the crowd, who all stopped in their game to drop their curtsies and make their bows; one might have thought that, like a tulip, she was rather frail in the stalk and feared to bend her back. The rose, the lily, and the pale hyacinth--yes, I saw them all three. Whose May-lambs were they one day to become, thought I; their mates would be proud knights--perhaps even princes! 'Whew!--whew!--fare away! Yes, the chariot bore them away, and the peasants whirled on in their dance. They played at "Riding the Summer into the village," to Borreby village, Tareby village, and many others. 'But that night when I rose,' said the wind, 'the noble lady laid herself down to rise no more; that came to her which comes to every one--there was nothing new about it. Waldemar Daa stood grave and silent for a time; "The proudest tree may bend, but it does not break," said something within him. The daughters wept, and every one else at the Castle was wiping their eyes; but Madam Daa had fared away, and I fared away too! Whew!--whew!' said the wind. [Illustration: _She played upon the ringing lute, and sang to its tones._] 'I came back again; I often came back across the island of Funen and the waters of the Belt, and took up my place on Borreby shore close to the great forest of oaks. The ospreys and the wood pigeons used to build in it, the blue raven and even the black stork! It was early in the year; some of the nests were full of eggs, while in others the young ones were just hatched. What a flying and screaming was there! Then came the sound of the axe, blow upon blow; the forest was to be felled. Waldemar Daa was about to build a costly ship, a three-decked man-of-war, which it was expected the king would buy. So the wood fell, the ancient landmark of the seaman, the home of the birds. The shrike was frightened away; its nest was torn down; the osprey and all the other birds lost their nests too, and they flew about distractedly, shrieking in their terror and anger. The crows and the jackdaws screamed in mockery, Caw! caw! Waldemar Daa and his three daughters stood in the middle of the wood among the workmen. They all laughed at the wild cries of the birds, except Anna Dorothea, who was touched by their distress, and when they were about to fell a tree which was half-dead, and on whose naked branches a black stork had built its nest, out of which the young ones were sticking their heads, she begged them with tears in her eyes to spare it. So the tree with the black stork's nest was allowed to stand. It was only a little thing. 'The chopping and the sawing went on--the three-decker was built. The master builder was a man of humble origin, but of noble loyalty; great power lay in his eyes and on his forehead, and Waldemar Daa liked to listen to him, and little Ida liked to listen too, the eldest fifteen-year-old daughter. But whilst he built the ship for her father, he built a castle in the air for himself, in which he and little Ida sat side by side as man and wife. This might also have happened if his castle had been built of solid stone, with moat and ramparts, wood and gardens. But with all his wisdom the shipbuilder was only a poor bird, and what business has a sparrow in a crane's nest? Whew! whew! I rushed away, and he rushed away, for he dared not stay, and little Ida got over it, as get over it she must. 'The fiery black horses stood neighing in the stables; they were worth looking at, and they were looked at to some purpose too. An admiral was sent from the King to look at the new man-of-war, with a view to purchasing it. The admiral was loud in his admiration of the horses. I heard all he said,' added the wind. 'I went through the open door with the gentlemen and scattered the straw like gold before their feet. Waldemar Daa wanted gold; the admiral wanted the black horses, and so he praised them as he did; but his hints were not taken, therefore the ship remained unsold. There it stood by the shore covered up with boards, like a Noah's Ark which never reached the water. Whew! whew! get along! get along! It was a miserable business. In the winter, when the fields were covered with snow and the Belt was full of ice-floes which I drove up on to the coast,' said the wind, 'the ravens and crows came in flocks, the one blacker than the other, and perched upon the desolate, dead ship by the shore. They screamed themselves hoarse about the forest which had disappeared, and the many precious birds' nests which had been devastated, leaving old and young homeless; and all for the sake of this old piece of lumber, the proud ship which was never to touch the water! I whirled the snow about till it lay in great heaps round the ship. I let it hear my voice, and all that a storm has to say, I know that I did my best to give it an idea of the sea. Whew! whew!' 'The winter passed by; winter and summer passed away! They come and go just as I do. The snow-flakes, the apple blossom, and the leaves fall, each in their turn. Whew! whew! they pass away, as men pass too! 'The daughters were still young. Little Ida, the rose, as lovely to look at as when the shipbuilder turned his gaze upon her. I often took hold of her long brown hair when she stood lost in thought by the apple-tree in the garden. She never noticed that I showered apple-blossom over her loosened hair; she only gazed at the red sunset against the golden background of the sky, and the dark trees and bushes of the garden. Her sister Johanna was like a tall, stately lily; she held herself as stiffly erect as her mother, and seemed to have the same dread of bending her stem. She liked to walk in the long gallery where the family portraits hung. The ladies were painted in velvet and silk, with tiny pearl embroidered caps on their braided tresses. Their husbands were all clad in steel, or in costly cloaks lined with squirrel skins and stiff blue ruffs; their swords hung loosely by their sides. Where would Johanna's portrait one day hang on these walls? What would her noble husband look like? These were her thoughts, and she even spoke them aloud; I heard her as I swept through the long corridor into the gallery, where I veered round again. 'Anna Dorothea, the pale hyacinth, was only a child of fourteen, quiet and thoughtful. Her large blue eyes, as clear as water, were very solemn, but childhood's smile still played upon her lips; I could not blow it away, nor did I wish to do so. I used to meet her in the garden, the ravine, and in the manor fields. She was always picking flowers and herbs, those she knew her father could use for healing drinks and potions. Waldemar Daa was proud and conceited, but he was also learned, and he knew a great deal about many things. One could see that, and many whispers went about as to his learning. The fire blazed in his stove even in summer, and his chamber door was locked. This went on for days and nights, but he did not talk much about it. One must deal silently with the forces of nature. He would soon discover the best of everything, the red, red gold! 'This was why his chimney flamed and smoked and sparkled. Yes, I was there, too,' said the wind. [Illustration: _I used to meet her in the garden, the ravine, and in the manor fields. She was always picking flowers and herbs, those she knew her father could use for healing drinks and potions._] 'Away with you, away! I sang in the back of the chimney. Smoke smoke, embers and ashes, that is all it will come to! You will burn yourself up in it. Whew! whew! away with it! But Waldemar Daa could not let it go. 'The fiery steeds in the stable, where were they? The old gold and silver plate in cupboard and chest, where was that? The cattle, the land, the castle itself? Yes, they could all be melted down in the crucible, but yet no gold would come. 'Barn and larder got emptier and emptier. Fewer servants; more mice. One pane of glass got broken and another followed it. There was no need for me to go in by the doors,' said the wind. 'A smoking chimney means a cooking meal, but the only chimney which smoked here swallowed up all the meals, all for the sake of the red gold. 'I blew through the castle gate like a watchman blowing his horn, but there was no watchman,' said the wind. 'I twisted round the weather-cock on the tower and it creaked as if the watchman up there was snoring, only there was no watchman. Rats and mice were the only inhabitants. Poverty laid the table; poverty lurked in wardrobe and larder. The doors fell off their hinges, cracks and crannies appeared everywhere; I went in and out,' said the wind, 'so I know all about it. 'The hair and the beard of Waldemar Daa grew grey, in the sorrow of his sleepless nights, amid smoke and ashes. His skin grew grimy and yellow, and his eyes greedy for gold, the long expected gold. 'I whistled through the broken panes and fissures; I blew into the daughters' chests where their clothes lay faded and threadbare; they had to last for ever. A song like this had never been sung over the cradles of these children. A lordly life became a woeful life! I was the only one to sing in the castle now,' said the wind. 'I snowed them up, for they said it gave warmth. They had no firewood, for the forest was cut down where they should have got it. There was a biting frost. Even I had to keep rushing through the crannies and passages to keep myself lively. They stayed in bed to keep themselves warm, those noble ladies. Their father crept about under a fur rug. Nothing to bite, and nothing to burn! a lordly life indeed! Whew! whew! let it go! But this was what Waldemar Daa could not do. '"After winter comes the spring," said he; "a good time will come after a time of need; but they make us wait their pleasure, wait! The castle is mortgaged, we are in extremities--and yet the gold will come--at Easter!" 'I heard him murmur to the spider's web.--"You clever little weaver! You teach me to persevere! If your web is broken, you begin at the beginning again and complete it! Broken again--and cheerfully you begin it over again. That is what one must do, and one will be rewarded!" 'It was Easter morning, the bells were ringing, and the sun was at play in the heavens. Waldemar Daa had watched through the night with his blood at fever pitch; boiling and cooling, mixing and distilling. I heard him sigh like a despairing soul; I heard him pray, and I felt that he held his breath. The lamp had gone out, but he never noticed it; I blew up the embers and they shone upon his ashen face, which took a tinge of colour from their light; his eyes started in their sockets, they grew larger and larger, as if they would leap out. 'Look at the alchemist's glass! something twinkles in it; it is glowing, pure and heavy. He lifted it with a trembling hand and shouted with a trembling voice: "Gold! gold!" He reeled, and I could easily have blown him over,' said the wind, 'but I only blew upon the embers, and followed him to the room where his daughters sat shivering. His coat was powdered with ash, as well as his beard and his matted hair. He drew himself up to his full height and held up his precious treasure, in the fragile glass: "Found! won! gold!" he cried, stretching up his hand with the glass which glittered in the sunbeams: his hand shook, and the alchemist's glass fell to the ground shivered into a thousand atoms. The last bubble of his welfare was shattered too. Whew! whew! fare away! and away I rushed from the goldmaker's home. [Illustration: _He lifted it with a trembling hand and shouted with a trembling voice: 'Gold! gold!'_] 'Late in the year, when the days were short and dark up here, and the fog envelops the red berries and bare branches with its cold moisture, I came along in a lively mood clearing the sky and snapping off the dead boughs. This is no great labour, it is true, yet it has to be done. Borreby Hall, the home of Waldemar Daa, was having a clean sweep of a different sort. The family enemy, Ov Ramel from Basness, appeared, holding the mortgage of the Hall and all its contents. I drummed upon the cracked window panes, beat against the decaying doors, and whistled through all the cracks and crannies, whew! I did my best to prevent Herr Ov taking a fancy to stay there. Ida and Anna Dorothea faced it bravely, although they shed some tears; Johanna stood pale and erect and bit her finger till it bled! Much that would help her! Ov Ramel offered to let them stay on at the Castle for Waldemar Daa's lifetime, but he got no thanks for his offer; I was listening. I saw the ruined gentleman stiffen his neck and hold his head higher than ever. I beat against the walls and the old linden trees with such force that the thickest branch broke, although it was not a bit rotten. It fell across the gate like a broom, as if some one was about to sweep; and a sweeping there was indeed to be. I quite expected it. It was a grievous day and a hard time for them, but their wills were as stubborn as their necks were stiff. They had not a possession in the world but the clothes on their backs; yes, one thing--an alchemist's glass which had been bought and filled with the fragments scraped up from the floor. The treasure which promised much and fulfilled nothing. Waldemar Daa hid it in his bosom, took his staff in his hand, and, with his three daughters, the once wealthy gentleman walked out of Borreby Hall for the last time. I blew a cold blast upon his burning cheeks, I fluttered his grey beard and his long white hair; I sang such a tune as only I could sing. Whew! whew! away with them! away with them! This was the end of all their grandeur. 'Ida and Ana Dorothea walked one on each side of him: Johanna turned round in the gateway, but what was the good of that? nothing could make their luck turn. She looked at the red stones of what had once been Marsk Stig's Castle. Was she thinking of his daughters? '"The elder took the younger by the hand, And out they roamed to a far-off land." Was she thinking of that song? Here there were three and their father was with them. They walked along the road where once they used to ride in their chariot. They trod it now as vagrants, on their way to a plastered cottage on Smidstrup Heath, which was rented at ten marks yearly. This was their new country seat with its empty walls and its empty vessels. The crows and the magpies wheeled screaming over their heads with their mocking "Caw, caw! Out of the nest, Caw, caw!" just as they screamed in Borreby Forest when the trees were felled. 'Herr Daa and his daughters must have noticed it. I blew into their ears to try and deaden the cries, which after all were not worth listening to. 'So they took up their abode in the plastered cottage on Smidstrup Heath, and I tore off over marshes and meadows, through naked hedges and bare woods, to the open seas and other lands. Whew! whew! away, away! and that for many years.' What happened to Waldemar Daa? What happened to his daughters? This is what the wind relates. 'The last of them I saw, yes, for the last time, was Anna Dorothea, the pale hyacinth. She was old and bent now; it was half a century later. She lived the longest, she had gone through everything. 'Across the heath, near the town of Viborg, stood the Dean's new, handsome mansion, built of red stone with toothed gables. The smoke curled thickly out of the chimneys. The gentle lady and her fair daughters sat in the bay window looking into the garden at the drooping thorns and out to the brown heath beyond. What were they looking at there? They were looking at a stork's nest on a tumble-down cottage; the roof was covered, as far as there was any roof to cover, with moss and house-leek; but the stork's nest made the best covering. It was the only part to which anything was done, for the stork kept it in repair. [Illustration: _Waldemar Daa hid it in his bosom, took his staff in his hand, and, with his three daughters, the once wealthy gentleman walked out of Borreby Hall for the last time._] 'This house was only fit to be looked at, not to be touched. I had to mind what I was about,' said the wind. 'The cottage was allowed to stand for the sake of the stork's nest; in itself it was only a scarecrow on the heath, but the dean did not want to frighten away the stork, so the hovel was allowed to stand. The poor soul inside was allowed to live in it; she had the Egyptian bird to thank for that; or was it payment for once having pleaded for the nest of his wild black brother in the Borreby Forest? Then, poor thing, she was a child, a delicate, pale hyacinth in a noble flower-garden. Poor Anna Dorothea; she remembered it all! Ah, human beings can sigh as well as the wind when it soughs through the rushes and reeds. 'Oh dear! oh dear! No bells rang over the grave of Waldemar Daa. No schoolboys sang when the former lord of Borreby Castle was laid in his grave. Well, everything must have an end, even misery! Sister Ida became the wife of a peasant, and this was her father's sorest trial. His daughter's husband a miserable serf, who might at any moment be ordered the punishment of the wooden horse by his lord. It is well that the sod covers him now, and you too, Ida! Ah yes! ah yes! Poor me! poor me! I still linger on. In Thy mercy release me, O Christ!' 'This was the prayer of Anna Dorothea, as she lay in the miserable hovel which was only left standing for the sake of the stork. 'I took charge of the boldest of the sisters,' said the wind. 'She had clothes made to suit her manly disposition, and took a place as a lad with a skipper. Her words were few and looks stubborn, but she was willing enough at her work. But with all her will she could not climb the rigging; so I blew her overboard before any one discovered that she was a woman, and I fancy that was not a bad deed of mine!' said the wind. 'On such an Easter morning as that on which Waldemar Daa thought he had found the red gold, I heard from beneath the stork's nest a psalm echoing through the miserable walls. It was Anna Dorothea's last song. There was no window; only a hole in the wall. The sun rose in splendour and poured in upon her; her eyes were glazed and her heart broken! This would have been so this morning whether the sun had shone upon her or not. The stork kept a roof over her head till her death! I sang at her grave,' said the wind, 'and I sang at her father's grave. I know where it is, and hers too, which is more than any one else knows. 'The old order changeth, giving place to the new. The old high-road now only leads to cultivated fields, while peaceful graves are covered by busy traffic on the new road. Soon comes Steam with its row of waggons behind it, rushing over the graves, forgotten, like the names upon them. Whew! whew! Let us be gone! This is the story of Waldemar Daa and his daughters. Tell it better yourselves, if you can,' said the wind, as it veered round. Then it was gone. [Illustration] Printed in Great Britain Text printed by T. and A. rewrite: When the wind sweeps across a field of grass, it creates gentle ripples like a lake; in a cornfield, it stirs great waves like the sea: this is the wind’s play. Then listen to the tales it tells; it sings them aloud, one melody among the forest trees, and another when confined within walls and their crevices. Do you see how the wind drives the fleecy clouds like a flock of sheep? Do you hear it howling at the open door like a watchman sounding his horn? And how it whistles down the chimneys, making the fire crackle and glow. How snug to sit by the fire’s warmth, hearing its stories! Let the wind speak for itself! It knows more adventures than all of us combined. Listen now:— “Whew!—Whew!—Away!” That was the chorus of its song. “Near the Great Belt stands an old manor with thick red walls,” says the wind. “I know every stone; I knew them when they were part of Marsk Stig’s Castle on the Ness. It fell. The stones were reused to build a new wall for a new castle elsewhere—Borreby Hall as it stands now. I have seen the noble folk of many lines who lived there, and now I shall tell of Waldemar Daa and his daughters! He carried himself proudly, being of royal descent! He knew more than hunting stags or draining goblets; he claimed skill in managing his affairs. His lady strode across polished floors in a gown of gold brocade; the tapestries were splendid, the furniture of costly carved wood. She brought much silver and gold plate, and the cellars held German ale when stocked. Black horses neighed in the stables; Borreby Hall was rich when wealth resided there. Then there were the children, three delicate maidens, Ida, Johanna and Anna Dorothea. I remember their names well. They were wealthy and high-born, reared in luxury! Whew!—whew!—away!” roared the wind, then continued. “I did not see here, as in other old castles, the lady among her maidens at the spinning-wheel. No, she played the ringing lute and sang. Her songs were not always old Danish airs, but in foreign tongues. All was lively and hospitable; noble guests came from afar; music sounded and flagons clashed, so loudly I could not drown them!” said the wind. “Here was arrogance and display in abundance; many lords, but the Lord had no place. Then came May-day evening!” said the wind. “I came from the west, having seen ships wrecked on Jutland’s coast. I raced over heaths and wooded shores, across Funen and the Great Belt, huffing and puffing. I rested on Zealand’s coast near Borreby Hall, where the fine oak forest still stood. Young bachelors gathered the longest, driest faggots they could find, took them to town, piled and lit them; then men and maidens danced and sang round the blaze. I lay still,” said the wind, “but I gently stirred a branch laid by the handsomest youth, and his billet blazed highest. He was chosen, earned the title ‘Buck of the Street,’ and picked his May-lamb from the girls. All was mirth, greater than within rich Borreby Hall. The great lady approached in her gilded chariot drawn by six horses, with her three delicate daughters—three lovely flowers: a rose, a lily, and a pale hyacinth. The mother herself was a splendid tulip; she ignored the crowd, who paused to curtsey and bow; one might think her, like a tulip, frail-stalked and fearing to bend. The rose, the lily, and the pale hyacinth—I saw them all. Whose May-lambs would they become? Their mates might be proud knights—even princes! Whew!—whew!—away! The chariot bore them off, and peasants danced on. They played at ‘Riding the Summer into the village,’ to Borreby, Tareby, and others. But that night when I rose,” said the wind, “the noble lady lay down to rise no more; that which comes to all came to her—nothing new. Waldemar Daa stood grave and silent awhile; ‘The proudest tree may bend but not break,’ he thought. The daughters wept; all at the Castle wiped their eyes; but Madam Daa had departed, and I departed too! Whew!—whew!” said the wind. “I returned; I often came back across Funen and the Belt, settling near Borreby’s oak forest. Ospreys, wood pigeons, blue ravens, even black storks nested there. Early in the year, nests held eggs or hatchlings. What flying and screaming! Then came axe blows; the forest was to be felled. Waldemar Daa meant to build a costly three-decked warship, hoping the king would buy it. So the wood fell, the seaman’s landmark, the birds’ home. The shrike fled; its nest destroyed; ospreys and others lost nests too, flying about distractedly, shrieking in terror and anger. Crows and jackdaws mocked, ‘Caw! caw!’ Waldemar Daa and his three daughters stood among workmen. All laughed at the birds’ cries except Anna Dorothea, moved by their distress. When they aimed to fell a half-dead tree where a black stork nested, young heads peeping out, she begged with tears to spare it. So the tree stood. A small thing. Chopping and sawing continued—the three-decker was built. The master builder was of humble birth but noble loyalty; power lay in his eyes and brow. Waldemar Daa liked listening to him, and little Ida liked listening too, the eldest, fifteen. While building the ship for her father, he built a castle in the air for himself, with him and little Ida as man and wife. This might have happened if his castle had stone walls, moats, ramparts, woods, and gardens. But with all his wisdom, the shipbuilder was a poor bird; what business has a sparrow in a crane’s nest? Whew! whew! I rushed away, and he rushed away, for he dared not stay, and little Ida got over it, as she must. The black horses neighed in the stables; worth seeing, and seen they were. An admiral came from the King to view the new warship. He admired the horses loudly. I heard all,” added the wind. “I went through the open door with the gentlemen, scattering straw like gold at their feet. Waldemar Daa wanted gold; the admiral wanted the black horses, so he praised them; but his hints were ignored, so the ship remained unsold. It stood shore-side, boarded up like a Noah’s Ark never touching water. Whew! whew! get along! A miserable affair. In winter, when fields were snow-clad and the Belt full of ice-floes I drove ashore,” said the wind, “ravens and crows came in flocks, blacker than each other, perching on the desolate, dead ship. They screamed hoarsely about the vanished forest, the many precious nests destroyed, leaving old and young homeless; all for this old lumber, the proud ship never to touch water! I whirled snow into heaps round the ship. I let it hear my voice, all a storm can say; I did my best to give it a taste of the sea. Whew! whew! Winter passed; winter and summer passed away! They come and go as I do. Snowflakes, apple blossoms, leaves fall in turn. Whew! whew! they pass, as men pass too! The daughters were still young. Little Ida, the rose, as lovely as when the shipbuilder gazed on her. I often caught her long brown hair as she stood thoughtful by the garden apple-tree. She never noticed I showered apple-blossom over her loosened hair; she gazed at the red sunset against gold sky, and the garden’s dark trees and bushes. Her sister Johanna was a tall, stately lily; she held herself stiffly erect as her mother, seeming to dread bending her stem. She liked walking the long gallery with family portraits. Ladies were painted in velvet and silk, pearl-embroidered caps on braided tresses. Their husbands wore steel or costly cloaks lined with squirrel fur and stiff blue ruffs; swords hung at their sides. Where would Johanna’s portrait hang? What would her noble husband look like? These were her thoughts, spoken aloud; I heard as I swept through the corridor into the gallery, where I veered round. Anna Dorothea, the pale hyacinth, was but fourteen, quiet and thoughtful. Her large blue eyes, clear as water, were solemn, but childhood’s smile still played on her lips; I could not blow it away, nor wished to. I met her in garden, ravine, and manor fields, always picking flowers and herbs she knew her father could use for healing drinks. Waldemar Daa was proud and vain, but learned, knowing much of many things. One could see that; whispers spoke of his learning. Fire blazed in his stove even in summer, his chamber door locked. This went on days and nights, but he spoke little of it. One must deal silently with nature’s forces. He would soon discover the best of all—red, red gold! So his chimney flamed, smoked, sparkled. Yes, I was there too,” said the wind. “Away with you, away! I sang behind the chimney. Smoke, embers, ashes—all it will come to! You will burn yourself. Whew! whew! away! But Waldemar Daa could not let go. The fiery steeds in the stable—where were they? The old gold and silver plate—where? Cattle, land, the castle itself? All could melt in the crucible, yet no gold came. Barn and larder emptied. Fewer servants; more mice. One pane broke, then another. I needed no doors,” said the wind. “A smoking chimney means cooking, but here it swallowed all meals, all for red gold. I blew through the castle gate like a watchman’s horn, but no watchman,” said the wind. “I twisted the weather-cock; it creaked as if the watchman snored, but none was there. Rats and mice alone lived. Poverty set the table; poverty lurked in wardrobe and larder. Doors fell off hinges; cracks appeared; I went in and out,” said the wind, “so I know all. Waldemar Daa’s hair and beard greyed in sorrowful sleepless nights amid smoke and ashes. His skin grew grimy and yellow, eyes greedy for the long-awaited gold. I whistled through broken panes and fissures; I blew into the daughters’ chests where clothes lay faded and threadbare; they had to last. Such a song had never been sung over their cradles. A lordly life turned woeful! I alone sang in the castle now,” said the wind. “I snowed them in, for they said it warmed. They had no firewood, the forest being cut. Biting frost. I rushed through crannies to stay lively. They stayed abed to keep warm, those noble ladies. Their father crept under a fur rug. Nothing to bite, nothing to burn! A lordly life indeed! Whew! whew! let it go! But Waldemar Daa could not. ‘After winter comes spring,’ he said; ‘good times follow need; but they make us wait. The castle is mortgaged, we are in extremities—yet gold will come—at Easter!’ I heard him murmur to a spider’s web: ‘You clever weaver! You teach perseverance! If your web breaks, you start anew and complete it! Broken again—cheerfully you begin over. That one must do, and be rewarded!’ It was Easter morning, bells ringing, sun playing in sky. Waldemar Daa watched through the night, blood fevered; boiling, cooling, mixing, distilling. I heard him sigh like a despairing soul; I heard him pray, felt him hold his breath. The lamp died, unnoticed; I blew embers glowing on his ashen face, tinged with light; eyes started, growing larger, as if to leap out. Look at the alchemist’s glass! Something twinkles, glowing, pure and heavy. He lifted it with trembling hand, shouted with trembling voice: ‘Gold! gold!’ He reeled; I could easily have blown him over,” said the wind, “but I only blew embers, followed him where his daughters sat shivering. His coat, beard, matted hair were ash-powdered. He drew up tall, held his precious treasure in fragile glass: ‘Found! won! gold!’ he cried, stretching hand with glass glittering in sunbeams: hand shook, glass fell, shattering. The last bubble of his welfare burst. Whew! whew! away! I rushed from the goldmaker’s home. Late in the year, when days were short, dark, fog enveloping red berries and bare branches with cold moisture, I came lively, clearing sky, snapping dead boughs. No great labour, yet needed. Borreby Hall had a clean sweep of another sort. The family enemy, Ove Ramel from Basness, appeared, holding the mortgage. I drummed cracked panes, beat decaying doors, whistled through cracks, whew! I tried to deter Herr Ove from staying. Ida and Anna Dorothea faced it bravely, though shedding tears; Johanna stood pale, erect, biting her finger till it bled! Much help! Ove Ramel offered they stay at the Castle for Waldemar Daa’s lifetime, but got no thanks; I listened. I saw the ruined gentleman stiffen his neck, hold his head higher. I beat walls and old linden trees so hard the thickest branch broke, though not rotten. It fell across the gate like a broom, as if to sweep; a sweeping there would be. I expected it. A grievous day, hard time, but their wills were stubborn as their necks stiff. They owned nothing but clothes on their backs; yes, one thing—an alchemist’s glass bought and filled with fragments scraped from the floor. The treasure promising much, fulfilling nothing. Waldemar Daa hid it in his bosom, took his staff, and with his three daughters, the once-wealthy gentleman walked out of Borreby Hall last. I blew a cold blast on his burning cheeks, fluttered his grey beard and long white hair; I sang a tune only I could. Whew! whew! away! This ended their grandeur. Ida and Anna Dorothea walked each side; Johanna turned at the gateway, but to what avail? Nothing could turn their luck. She looked at red stones of what was once Marsk Stig’s Castle. Was she thinking of his daughters? ‘The elder took the younger by the hand, And out they roamed to a far-off land.’ Was she thinking that? Here were three, their father with them. They trod the road where once they rode in chariot. Now vagrants, heading to a plastered cottage on Smidstrup Heath, rented at ten marks yearly. Their new country seat with empty walls and vessels. Crows and magpies wheeled overhead, mocking ‘Caw, caw! Out of the nest!’ as in Borreby Forest when trees fell. Herr Daa and his daughters must have noticed. I blew in their ears to deaden the cries, worthless anyway. So they dwelt in the plastered cottage on Smidstrup Heath, and I tore over marshes, meadows, naked hedges, bare woods, to open seas and other lands. Whew! whew! away, away! for many years.” What became of Waldemar Daa? What of his daughters? The wind tells. “The last I saw, yes, last time, was Anna Dorothea, the pale hyacinth. She was old, bent; half a century later. She lived longest, having endured all. Across the heath, near Viborg, stood the Dean’s new, handsome mansion of red stone with toothed gables. Smoke curled thick from chimneys. The gentle lady and fair daughters sat in the bay window, looking into garden at drooping thorns, out to brown heath. What did they see? A stork’s nest on a tumble-down cottage; roof covered, where roof remained, with moss and house-leek; but the stork’s nest made the best cover. Only that part was tended, for the stork kept it repaired. This house was only to be looked at, not touched. I had to mind,” said the wind. “The cottage stood for the stork’s nest; itself a scarecrow on the heath, but the dean did not wish to scare the stork, so the hovel remained. The poor soul inside lived there; she had the Egyptian bird to thank; or was it payment for once pleading for its wild black brother’s nest in Borreby Forest? Then, poor thing, she was a child, a delicate pale hyacinth in a noble garden. Poor Anna Dorothea; she remembered all! Ah, humans can sigh as wind soughs through rushes. Oh dear! No bells rang over Waldemar Daa’s grave. No schoolboys sang when the former lord of Borreby was buried. Well, all ends, even misery! Sister Ida wed a peasant, her father’s sorest trial. His daughter’s husband a miserable serf, who might be ordered the wooden horse by his lord. Well the sod covers him now, and you, Ida! Ah yes! Poor me! I linger. In Thy mercy release me, O Christ!’ This was Anna Dorothea’s prayer in the miserable hovel left standing for the stork. ‘I took charge of the boldest sister,’ said the wind. ‘She dressed mannishly, worked as a lad with a skipper. Words few, looks stubborn, but willing. Yet she could not climb rigging; so I blew her overboard before any discovered she was a woman, and I fancy that not a bad deed!’ said the wind. ‘On such an Easter morning as when Waldemar Daa thought he had found red gold, I heard from beneath the stork’s nest a psalm echoing through miserable walls. Anna Dorothea’s last song. No window; only a wall hole. The sun rose splendidly, pouring in; her eyes glazed, heart broken! So it would have been whether sun shone or not. The stork kept a roof over her head till death! I sang at her grave,’ said the wind, ‘and at her father’s. I know where both lie, more than any. The old order changes, giving place to new.
